prompt: Payroll is mission-critical at Serra Alta: get it wrong and 3,200 people are paid late. Why does the lesson still put it among the things to buy?
hint: Two axes, and only one of them decides the sourcing.

choices.text: Because criticality settles how carefully it is done, and payroll gives Serra Alta no edge over another dairy
choices.why: Right: Moore's two axes are separate. Paying people well wins no farm and no shelf, so it is context, and being critical only raises the bar for whoever provides it.

choices.text: Because payroll costs so little that building it would waste money
choices.why: Cost is not the argument. The lesson puts payroll with the things to buy because doing it better earns nothing, whatever it costs.

choices.text: Because mission-critical work belongs with a vendor rather than the company's own team
choices.why: Criticality does not choose the source. Farm-payment policy is also critical, and it stays Serra Alta's own.

choices.text: Because a system of record changes too slowly to be worth building
choices.why: Pace layers are about how a system is governed, not whether to build it; Serra Alta's records change slowly because they must be right.

prompt: Cláudia's committee revises the quality bonus tables twice a year. Put through the copy test, which part of farm payment is core?
hint: What would a competitor still lack after buying the same software?

choices.text: The calculation that applies the tables to each farm's litres, because it handles the farms' money
choices.why: Handling money makes it mission-critical, not core. Every dairy does that multiplication, and several products already do it.

choices.text: Both halves, since the policy cannot change without changing the code
choices.why: That is true only of a system where the policy is code. In a product with rule tables the policy is data, and the split is the whole point.

choices.text: The policy: the bands and bonuses
choices.why: Right: a competitor who bought the same product would still not have Serra Alta's tables, its farms' history or its technicians.

choices.text: Neither, because every dairy in Brazil pays for quality somehow
choices.why: Every dairy pays for quality, but not with the same tables; the tables are what the best farms compare.

prompt: Which of these justify building something that is context? Choose all that apply.
hint: A reason that counts can be checked by somebody else.

choices.text: We could build a better version than any product
choices.why: A statement about the builders rather than the business, and true only of the part they can see.

choices.text: No product expresses a rule the business will not give up, and the gap is too wide to extend beside
choices.why: Yes: a fit-gap measures it, and it is the strongest of the four.

choices.text: Products on the market fail a legal requirement that applies to the company
choices.why: Yes: checkable against the law and the products' documentation.

choices.text: Building avoids depending on a vendor
choices.why: Every option depends on somebody; a build depends on the few people who understand it. Section 05 prices dependence instead.

choices.text: At the company's volume every per-unit price is absurd
choices.why: Yes: the arithmetic of a per-unit metric at your scale is a reason anybody can check.

prompt: Option A's year-3 price is R$ 26 per farm per month, and Serra Alta has 2,100 farms that year. What is the year-3 subscription?
hint: Price × farms × months.

prompt: Option A spends R$ 2,044,500 in year 1 and R$ 3,835,700 over the three years. What percentage of the spending falls in year 1, to one decimal place?
hint: Year 1 over the total, times 100.

prompt: Serra Alta's sheet puts each payment in the calendar year it is made, with no year-0 column for what is paid before go-live. Why?
hint: When does each option start running?

choices.text: A year-0 column would count the one-off costs twice
choices.why: It would count them once, in a different place. The problem is what that place hides, not double counting.

choices.text: Calendar years make discounting to present value unnecessary
choices.why: Marcos's team discounts the calendar years too; the sheet stays in plain reais because discounting did not change the order.

choices.text: The options start running at different times, and a shared year 0 would hide the year the build spends before paying anybody
choices.why: Right: year 0 works when every option goes live on the same day. Here A pays farms in month 10 and C in month 16.

choices.text: Finance teams have stopped accepting a year-0 column in a cost of ownership, because auditors read it as money spent before a contract
choices.why: They use it widely, and the lesson says so. It is the wrong shape for this comparison, not a banned one.

prompt: On the sheet, a line that costs nothing gets a typed ___: an empty cell says nobody looked.
hint: A number, not a blank.

prompt: The vendor's proposal for A said R$ 2,070,000. The full sheet, exit included, says R$ 4,233,500. How much of A's cost was not on the proposal?
hint: The sheet minus the proposal.

prompt: Building C costs R$ 2,100,000. Using Serra Alta's planning assumption for maintenance, what does keeping it running and changing cost a year?
hint: A fifth of the build, every year.

prompt: Joana's first estimate for C was seven people for twelve months. Which of these were missing from it? Choose all that apply.
hint: Everything that happens after month 12.

choices.text: Somebody on call at night during payment week
choices.why: Yes: R$ 10,000 a month on C's sheet, because the payment run on the 10th happens whether or not it is convenient.

choices.text: The subscription paid while the product is being implemented
choices.why: That is a buyer's blind spot. A build has no subscription to pay.

choices.text: Maintenance for every year after go-live
choices.why: Yes: 20% of the build a year, R$ 840,000 over the 24 months after go-live.

choices.text: A cap on the price rise at renewal
choices.why: A contract clause for the bought option; there is nothing to renew in a build.

choices.text: Security patches and a yearly penetration test
choices.why: Yes: a system holding 1,900 farmers' bank accounts needs both, and the test is R$ 40,000 a year.

prompt: A second vendor quotes R$ 22 per registered farm per month, against the first vendor's R$ 25 per active farm. Coleta still holds records for farms that stopped delivering years ago. What should Joana find out before calling the second quote cheaper?
hint: Read the metric before the price.

choices.text: Whether the second vendor's price per farm falls as Serra Alta adds the hundred farms a year its milk plan expects
choices.why: Volume discounts matter later. The first question is what is being counted at all.

choices.text: How many registered records there are, since farms that no longer deliver would be billed too
choices.why: Right: at R$ 22 a farm, a few hundred stale records erase the difference. Lesson 14's profiling gives the count.

choices.text: Whether R$ 22 per registered farm is below what SAP would charge to hold the same farm records itself
choices.why: SAP is not selling this metric; the comparison is between the two vendors' counts.

choices.text: Whether the second vendor's product can run on Coleta's IBM i
choices.why: Coleta is being retired; the new product will not run on its machine in either case.

prompt: Leaving A at the end of month 36 costs R$ 30,000 of export, three overlap months at R$ 26 × 2,100 farms, 60% of the R$ 240,000 integration line rebuilt, and R$ 60,000 of retraining. What is the exit line?
hint: Four parts; the overlap is three months of subscription.

prompt: B has the smallest exit of the three options, R$ 190,000. What is the main reason?
hint: What stays when the farm payment leaves B?

choices.text: SAP charges nothing to terminate custom development
choices.why: There is no termination fee in any of the three exits at the end of a term; this does not separate B.

choices.text: B has so few integrations that nothing needs rebuilding
choices.why: R$ 90,000 of B's integrations is rebuilt; the line is smaller, not empty.

choices.text: Custom code written in SAP moves easily into another product
choices.why: It does not; the rules would be written again in the next system, which is that system's cost.

choices.text: SAP stays, so there is no subscription to overlap
choices.why: Right: Serra Alta is already locked into SAP, and lock-in it already holds costs nothing extra to add to. B's lock-in shows in its upgrades line instead.

prompt: Suppose A's contract had no cap at renewal. The first term ends in December 2028 and needs six months' notice. In August 2028 the vendor announces a 30% rise for year 3. Where does Serra Alta stand?
hint: Count back six months from the end of the term.

choices.text: It can give notice now and leave at the end of December
choices.why: Notice for a December exit had to be given by the end of June; in August it is two months late.

choices.text: The June notice date has passed, so year 3 is renewed at whatever the vendor now asks
choices.why: Right: the notice period is lock-in as a date. That is why the record puts a review every year before 31 May.

choices.text: It keeps the old price for year 3, because a renewal price is fixed on the day the original contract was signed
choices.why: Only a clause fixes a renewal price; this contract, by supposition, has none.

choices.text: It can leave at once by paying a small termination fee
choices.why: Leaving early means paying the rest of the term, which here is year 3 itself; there is no small fee.

prompt: Match each part of an exit to what it pays for.
hint: The next system's own costs are on the next system's sheet.

pairs.right: getting the history out in a form another system can load
the old system running during the parallel run
interfaces that spoke to the old system
drivers and office staff learning a new screen

prompt: C's TCO is R$ 4,679,000. If the build takes 18 months instead of 12, the team costs 6 × R$ 175,000 more, maintenance falls by R$ 210,000, operation by R$ 60,000 and infrastructure by R$ 36,000, and Coleta costs R$ 90,000 more. What is C's TCO then?
hint: Add the net change to the old total.

prompt: With a 15% rise at renewal, A's year-3 price is R$ 28.75 per farm per month. What is A's year-3 subscription for 2,100 farms?
hint: Twelve months of it.

prompt: Section 06 tests two soft assumptions. Which one changes the order of the three options, and how?
hint: Look at which totals cross each other.

choices.text: The 15% renewal rise, which puts A behind C
choices.why: A rises to R$ 4,320,125 and stays R$ 358,875 below C; it would take a price of R$ 40.14 for A to lose.

choices.text: The 50% longer build, which puts C above B while A stays first
choices.why: Right: C rises by R$ 834,000 to R$ 5,513,000, above B's R$ 5,261,000.

choices.text: The 50% longer build, which brings C level with A
choices.why: A longer build makes C more expensive, not cheaper; it moves away from A.

choices.text: Neither: each moves one total, and the order of the three is the same in both cases
choices.why: One of them does change it, behind A: C and B swap places.

prompt: At month 6, B had spent the least of the three options. Why does that not make B the cheapest?
hint: When does B's biggest line happen?

choices.text: The exit, added in month 36, pushes B above the others
choices.why: B has the smallest exit of the three; it is ahead long before month 36.

choices.text: B's licences are per farm, so they grow with every farm added after month 6
choices.why: B's licences are a flat R$ 15,000 a month; the per-farm metric is A's.

choices.text: Its custom development runs to month 16, so it passes C in month 13
choices.why: Right: at R$ 120,000 a month it ends highest, and the curve's shape is the argument. A comparison taken early reads the cheapest start, not the cheapest option.

choices.text: A's subscription is paid in advance, which makes A look dearer at month 6 than it is
choices.why: A pays its subscription month by month on this sheet; nothing about A is distorted at month 6.

prompt: Put these parts of Joana's buy-or-build record in the order a reader needs them.
hint: Nobody can judge a choice before knowing what was asked and what it rests on.
trap: Putting the decision first makes the options read as justification written afterwards, and the weak point only makes sense once the choice it weakens is stated.

prompt: Joana set the renewal trigger at R$ 32, below the R$ 40.14 ___ at which A loses to C, because notice has to be given six months ahead.
hint: The price at which the two totals are equal.

prompt: Nobody in the meeting asked for it. Why does Joana write the weak point into her own recommendation?
hint: Think of the reader in 2029.

choices.text: It protects her if the decision later goes wrong
choices.why: That is a reason somebody gives, and it makes the record about the author. The record is for the reader who has to act on it.

choices.text: Serra Alta's template has a field for risks
choices.why: The lesson's record follows Nygard's form plus four additions; the reason for this one is trust, not a field.

choices.text: A reader who finds a weakness the author left out stops trusting the numbers beside it
choices.why: Right: a recommendation with no weak point reads as advocacy, and naming it puts the risk where the committee can watch it.

choices.text: It lets the CFO choose a different option if the risk looks too high
choices.why: Marcos can choose differently either way; the weak point is written so the choice he makes is informed and its risk watched.

prompt: Match each cost line to the option whose sheet carries it.
hint: Who pays per farm, who pays at each SAP upgrade, who pays a fifth of the build?

pairs.left: R$ 25 per active farm per month
custom code tested again at each S/4HANA upgrade
maintenance at 20% of the build a year

prompt: In year 3, A spends R$ 923,200 and C spends R$ 748,000. At month 36, C has spent R$ 536,300 more than A. If year 3's costs repeated every year, how many more years would C need to catch up? Answer to two decimal places.
hint: The gap divided by what C saves each year.

prompt: A loses to C when the 31,500 farm-months at the renewal price cost R$ 445,500 more than they do at R$ 26. At what price per farm per month does that happen? Answer to the cent.
hint: Divide, then add to R$ 26.

prompt: A transport company's freight-audit system checks every carrier's invoice. Every transport company does it, a wrong payment is serious, and a product fits 48 of its 50 rules. The in-house team says it could build a better one in nine months. What does this lesson recommend?
hint: Place it on both axes first, then think about the two rules.

choices.text: Build, because a mission-critical system should stay in the company's hands
choices.why: Criticality sets how carefully it is done, not who does it; payroll is critical and bought everywhere.

choices.text: Buy it, and modify the product's code for the two rules so it fits exactly
choices.why: Modifying the product turns every release into a project; lesson 1's rings say extend beside, never modify.

choices.text: Build, because nine months is shorter than most implementations
choices.why: Nine months is the builders' estimate of the first line; maintenance, on-call and upgrades follow every year after it.

choices.text: Buy it, extend beside it for the two rules, and price every line of both options before signing
choices.why: Right: it is context, so building needs a reason, and 'we could build it better' is not one. The sheet still has to be done.
